# Use Qwen to Write a Clear Project Update Email for Your Manager

> **In short:** Open Qwen in your browser, paste three quick notes — what's done, what's stuck, and what's next — then ask it to write a 30-second project update. You'll get a clean email draft in about a minute.

By the end of this short walkthrough, you'll have a tight project update email drafted in a fraction of the time it would normally take you. This guide is for anyone who has ever stared at a blank email trying to summarize a week of work into a few polite sentences — and Qwen (Alibaba's AI assistant) is a perfectly capable helper for the job.

## Before you start
- A free Qwen account. Sign up with an email address, Google, or Apple on the Qwen chat page. The free tier is enough for this task.
- A web browser on a phone or computer — Qwen runs in any modern browser.
- About five minutes of quiet time.
- Three short notes about your project: what's done, what's blocked, and what's next. Even half-sentences work — Qwen will tidy them up.

## Step 1 — Open Qwen in your browser
Type the address of the Qwen chat page into your browser's address bar and press Enter. The page loads with a mostly empty screen and a long text box near the bottom. The box is often labeled something like "Message" or "Send a message" — your version may say something slightly different, but the box itself is the part that matters. If you can see a **Sign in** or **Log in** button at the top right, you'll need an account before you can send anything; Step 2 covers that.

💬 Example: N/A for this step — just opening the page.

You'll know it worked when you can see a text input box at the bottom and (after signing in) a conversation area above it.

## Step 2 — Sign in so your chats are saved
Click the **Sign in** button near the top of the page. A small window or panel appears with options to continue with email, Google, or Apple — pick whichever is fastest for you. Follow the prompts to either create a free account or log in to one you already have. When it's done, your name, an avatar, or a small profile icon appears in the corner of the page.

If you don't see "Sign in" but you're not in a chat yet, look for a button labeled **Log in**, **Get started**, or your profile picture. Some browser versions drop you straight into a chat as a guest — that's fine for a one-off draft, but signing in lets you come back to the conversation later if you need to.

💬 Example: N/A for this step — just signing in.

You'll know it worked when the page reloads and shows your account info, and the chat box is ready to receive a message.

## Step 3 — Paste your three rough notes
Click inside the text box at the bottom of the page. Now type, or paste, your three short notes — done, stuck, next. They don't need to be sentences; bullet points, fragments, even one-word reminders are fine. The goal here is to get your real thoughts out of your head and onto the screen. Qwen is a large language model (an AI trained to read and write text — think of it as the engine behind most modern AI assistants), and it reads whatever you give it as raw source material.

If your notes are scattered across a notebook, a Slack thread, or a meeting transcript, copy them in as a single block. Don't try to polish them — that's Qwen's job, not yours.

💬 Example:
Done: shipped the new onboarding flow on Tuesday. Stuck: waiting on legal review for the privacy notice. Next: design review on Friday, Maria owns the agenda.

You'll know it worked when all three of your notes are visible in the text box and the send button (usually a small arrow or paper-plane icon) becomes active.

## Step 4 — Ask Qwen to write the email
Now you tell Qwen what you want — this kind of instruction is called a **prompt**, which is just a fancy word for "the thing you ask the AI." Press Enter or click the send button. Qwen starts typing its reply within a second or two, and a complete email draft appears in the conversation area within about ten seconds. Read it once, top to bottom.

If the first draft sounds too formal, too casual, or doesn't quite match how your team communicates, don't worry — Step 5 fixes that. For now, just check that the three facts you gave it (done, stuck, next) all made it into the email and that nothing important got dropped.

💬 Example:
Turn these notes into a short project update email to my manager. Keep it under 120 words, friendly-professional tone, one short paragraph for each section (Done, Stuck, Next). No subject line needed.

You'll know it worked when you can see a complete email draft in the conversation with your three notes turned into proper sentences.

## Step 5 — Tweak the draft until it sounds like you
Type a follow-up message asking Qwen to adjust the draft. It will replace the previous version with a new one in the same conversation. You can ask for it to be shorter, warmer, more direct, more formal, or to mention a specific date or person. Be specific about what you want changed — vague requests get vague results. The first version is rarely the last one; expect to do two or three rounds of small adjustments.

If something important is missing — a deadline, a person's name, a number — just type "add that the design review is Friday at 2pm" and Qwen will fold it in. Remember: Qwen can only work with what you tell it. It doesn't know your real project, your real colleagues, or your real deadlines, so it cannot fill in facts you didn't share.

💬 Example:
Shorter — aim for 80 words max. Drop the "Hope this helps" opener. Add that the design review is Friday at 2pm.

You'll know it worked when the new draft matches how you'd actually write the email and includes every fact your manager needs.

## Step 6 — Copy the draft and paste it into your email
Find the **copy** button near the email draft — it's usually a small icon shaped like two overlapping squares, sitting at the top or bottom of Qwen's reply. Click it. If you can't find a copy button, click and drag to highlight the whole draft, then press Ctrl+C (Windows) or Cmd+C (Mac). Open your email client — Gmail, Outlook, anything — start a new message to your manager, paste the text with Ctrl+V or Cmd+V, add a subject line, and send.

Qwen can draft the email, but it can't send it for you — the final send is always yours, and so is the responsibility for what's in it.

💬 Example: N/A — this is a copy/paste action.

You'll know it worked when the email draft is sitting in your email client, ready for you to add a subject line and hit send.

## Common mistakes
- **Giving Qwen too little to work with.** If you only paste one vague sentence like "stuff is going OK, some blockers," the email will be vague too. The more concrete your three notes, the better the draft. Numbers, dates, and names are gold here.
- **Sending the first draft without reading.** Qwen sometimes smooths over real problems or invents polite-sounding filler. Always read the final version as if a colleague wrote it — fix anything that's wrong, missing, or too corporate.
- **Writing for a manager who already knows everything.** If your manager is up to speed, ask for a one-line status. If they need context, ask for a fuller version. State who the reader is in the prompt, and Qwen will adjust.
- **Forgetting who owns the next step.** A "Next" section without an owner creates confusion. Always include the name of the person responsible for the next action — otherwise your manager has to email you back to ask.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** The same three-notes trick works for any short status-style message — a volunteer group update, a family trip recap, a quick summary of a doctor's appointment to send to a relative. Anywhere you'd normally write "here's what's happening," Qwen can tidy it up.
- **For your business or work:** This is the easiest way to write weekly status updates, project briefs, and stakeholder check-ins without sitting in front of a blank screen. Once you get the hang of the three-notes format, you can draft an update in under five minutes — and the output is consistent in tone every week.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't overthink the first prompt. Open Qwen, paste whatever you have, and ask for a short email. You can refine from there. The hardest part is starting — Qwen does the rest.

## Try it now
Open the Qwen chat page, paste your last three project notes (done, stuck, next) into the text box, and ask Qwen to turn them into an email of 100 words or fewer. Read the result, tweak one small thing, then copy it into your next status update. You'll have a real, sendable draft in about three minutes.
